title: Encode and Decode Strings
summary: Design a class `Codec`. `encode(strs)` packs a list of strings into a single string, and `decode(s)` takes a string that `encode` made and returns the original list exactly: same strings, same order, empty strings included. The strings may contain any ASCII character, so no character is safe to use as a plain separator. The format is yours to choose.

examples.input: encode(["4#ab", "", "hello, world"]), then decode what it returned
examples.explanation: The encoded string can look like anything, as long as decode turns it back into the same three strings, including the empty one.

examples.input: encode([]), then decode what it returned
examples.explanation: An empty list must come back empty, not as [""].

constraints: strs[i] may contain any ASCII character, digits and # included
decode is only called on a string that encode returned

approaches.twist: Write each string's length and a '#' in front of it, so decode reads the length and copies exactly that many characters.
Join the strings with a separator and escape every separator and escape character inside them, then undo the escaping when decoding.
approaches.note: Works if every separator and every escape character is escaped, but it's easy to get wrong and decoding must scan for escapes. A length header has no special cases.

signals.meaning: A separator can show up inside a string, so splitting on it would cut a string in two. Record each string's length in front of it instead; then nothing inside the string is ever read as a separator.
An empty string still gets a header, 0#, so it survives the round trip, and an empty list encodes to an empty string.
Collect the pieces in a list and glue them with "".join(): adding to a string over and over can copy it each time.

constraintReading: Up to 200 strings of up to 200 characters, so n, the total length, is at most 4·10⁴: any single pass is fast. The real constraint is the alphabet: since any ASCII character can appear, a plain separator fails on some input, so the format has to say where each string ends before the decoder reaches it. Both methods should touch each character once: O(n) time and O(n) space for the result.

hints.clarify: Can a string contain the character you'd like to split on? Yes: any character can appear. Try joining ["a,b", "c"] with commas: you get "a,b,c", and splitting it gives three strings, not two. And [] versus [""]: both must come back exactly, so they need different encodings.
hints.approach: Prefix scan with a length header. Write each string's length and a `#` in front of it: ["a#b", ""] becomes "3#a#b0#". To decode, keep a position `i`. Find the first `#` at or after `i`; the digits between are the length n. Copy the n characters after the `#`, then jump `i` past them. Each string starts exactly where the lengths before it add up to, so a `#` or a digit inside a string is copied, never read as a header.
hints.whyNot: A plain separator breaks as soon as a string contains it, and here any character can. Escaping the separator inside the strings works, but you must escape the escape character too, and decoding has to undo both. Turning the list into JSON or a repr hands the escaping to a library; the length header needs no library and has no special cases.

slots.setup: In `encode`, an empty list of pieces. In `decode`, an empty result list and a position `i` = 0 at the start of the encoded string.
slots.loop: `encode` visits each string once. `decode` keeps going while `i` is still inside the encoded string.
slots.update: In `decode`, find the next `#` from `i`; the digits before it give the length n. After copying, move `i` to just past the copied characters.
slots.record: `encode` adds the length, a `#` and the string itself as one piece. `decode` copies the n characters after the `#` into the result.
slots.return: `encode` joins the pieces into one string. `decode` returns its list once `i` reaches the end; an empty string decodes to an empty list, because the loop never runs.

solution.explanation: `encode` writes each character once, plus a header of a few digits per string, and `"".join` builds the result in one go: O(n) time. In `decode`, the search for `#` reads only the digits of one header, and each string is copied once, so the pointer `i` only moves forward: O(n) time. Both build an output the size of the input: O(n) space. The header's digits can't contain a `#`, so the first `#` after `i` always ends the header, even when the string after it is full of `#` and digits.

events.label: header
events.say: {word!r} has {len(word)} characters, so its piece is {len(word)}, then '#', then the string itself

events.label: join
events.say: Glue the {len(parts)} pieces into one string

events.label: find #
events.say: A header starts at i = {i}. Find the first '#' from there

events.label: length
events.say: s[{i}:{j}] is {s[i:j]!r}, so the next string has {s[i:j]} characters

events.label: copy
events.say: Copy the {n} characters after the '#': {s[j + 1 : j + 1 + n]!r}. Any '#' or digit inside them is just text

events.label: return
events.say: i reached the end of s, so every string is back: {len(strs)} of them

predict.ask: Where is the '#' that ends this header?
Where will i be once this string is copied?
